claims.text: The initial material is a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with distinct interphase boundaries.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature cause accelerated degradation in multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloys.
Localized galvanic interactions occur at interphase boundaries.
Mechanical abrasion exposes fresh reactive surfaces.
The combination of galvanic interactions and mechanical abrasion nucleates micro-cracks.
Interphase boundaries act as sites of stress concentration.
Differential electrochemical potentials between phases establish localized galvanic cells at interphase boundaries.
Mechanical abrasion of the localized galvanic cells accelerates corrosion on freshly exposed surfaces.
Mechanical loading produces stress-induced micro-cracking at or near interphase boundaries.
Wear-induced surface exposure and galvanic corrosion act synergistically to amplify total degradation.
Relative to a homogenized alloy with minimized interphase boundaries, the multi-phase alloy will show greater total degradation under identical test conditions.
The multi-phase alloy will have a higher wear rate because weakened interphase zones promote material removal.
The multi-phase alloy will have a higher corrosion rate because of localized galvanic interactions.
The proposed mechanism requires an environment sufficiently aggressive to sustain active electrochemical reactions.
The proposed mechanism requires wear sufficient to periodically expose fresh surfaces at interphase boundaries.
The magnitude of the wear and corrosion increase varies with microstructural heterogeneity and test-environment details.
A comparison between the multi-phase alloy and a homogenized variant under identical simultaneous wear-corrosion conditions can test the proposed mechanism.
Similar degradation rates and localized damage mechanisms in the homogenized and multi-phase samples would falsify the proposed interphase-boundary mechanism.
